title: Choose the visual world
question: Pick the visual language for your household observatory. Every option keeps the data real; the difference is how the home becomes legible.

options.label: House Cutaway
options.lineage: architectural sections and electrical drafting plates
options.thesis: The home becomes a readable instrument: circuits, devices, and money routes drawn as one cutaway.
options.viewport: A wide cutaway of the household's energy plane anchors the first viewport; a narrow cost rail reads like a stamped instrument schedule.
options.risk: Reads like an engineering diagram if the human household story is not named beside the measurements.

raised.raise: Every chart now uses hard-edged planes and a disciplined depth order so signal never dissolves into decoration.
The opening read follows a practiced cross-check: household total, device share, rate, then financial consequence.
Source state and data freshness stay explicit in the interface instead of hiding behind polished summaries.

options.label: Household Observatory
options.thesis: Every source is a body in one private sky, with long-range patterns made visible instead of flattened.
options.viewport: A constellation-like yearly energy trace sits beside bright current facts; device and wallet signals orbit the same date spine.
options.risk: The metaphor is familiar in data products; it must stay grounded in real household labels and precise units.

options.label: Source Archive Wall
options.lineage: sneaker archive walls and stacked cardboard boxes
options.thesis: Each source becomes a physical archive box that can be pulled forward for detail.
options.viewport: A wall of source boxes indexes ISMRT, Bneta, and financial streams before a selected box opens into its trend detail.
options.risk: The fashion-archive carrier makes the household story less identifiable.
options.case: Fuses cleanly as a provenance-first archive, but loses on audience identification and clarity: household data should feel lived-in, not merchandised.
options.kept: Source labels become physical-looking index tabs with exact units and dates.

options.label: Gravity Garden
options.thesis: Usage flows toward the things that pull on the household: devices, weather, and bills.
options.viewport: A living flow field bends daily usage toward the device or charge responsible, with anomalies changing the trajectory.
options.risk: Motion becomes the story and exact readings become secondary.
options.case: Strong at showing relationships, weak at read-only trust: the visitor should inspect measured facts before exploring a metaphor.
options.kept: Directional flow is donated to comparison charts: cost lines can visibly pull away from usage lines when tariffs change.

options.label: Signal Captions
options.lineage: broadcast telop fields and live comic captions
options.thesis: The dashboard speaks in timed annotations, making unusual household moments impossible to miss.
options.viewport: Outlier days enter as large caption cards over the trend field: automation left on, guests arrived, or the geyser went cold.
options.risk: Entertainment energy can make financial and utility facts feel unserious.
options.case: Good for annotations but loses both audience identification and product clarity as the primary world.
options.kept: Human context events get a restrained caption treatment rather than disappearing into a tooltip.

options.label: Industrial Plate
options.lineage: precisionist industrial paintings and hard-edged plant diagrams
options.thesis: A few decisive planes turn a messy household into a calm, inspectable machine.
options.viewport: Large geometric planes carry the household total, device share, and monthly charge; each selected plane opens its underlying series.
options.risk: It can look like an industrial operations room instead of a couple's home.
options.case: Competitive: strong clarity and visual discipline, but its audience identity is colder than the household brief.
options.kept: Hard-edged geometric chart regions and a single-plane focus state raise the assigned direction.

options.label: Night Instrument Six-Pack
options.lineage: small-aircraft cockpit gauges and night flight panels
options.thesis: Six calm instruments hold trust through noise; the eye sweeps them in a practiced order.
options.viewport: Household kWh, espresso share, current rate, monthly cost, water invoice, and data freshness form a single cross-check row.
options.risk: A cockpit metaphor can overstate the operational seriousness of domestic data.
options.case: Competitive: best immediate scan order, but less expressive for source provenance and future financial surfaces.
options.kept: Calibrated ticks, quiet warning states, and cross-check reading order become the dashboard's control grammar.

options.label: One-Bit Desktop
options.lineage: early one-bit desktops and dithered utility software
options.thesis: Owned data deserves visible mechanics: windows, selections, raw records, and no opaque surface.
options.viewport: A source desktop opens windows for energy, money, and raw events, with a selected row always traceable to its origin.
options.risk: The novelty of the rendering language competes with the data.
options.case: Fuses well with ownership and auditability, but loses on first-glance clarity and household warmth.
options.kept: Explicit source state, selected-row lineage, and no hidden data transformations.

canonCard.label: The category standard
canonCard.thesis: A conventional SaaS dashboard: sidebar, KPI cards, line charts, and a neutral data table.
canonCard.viewport: A familiar overview page makes the latest KPIs and a single trend chart immediately scannable.
canonCard.risk: It would be legible but forgettable, and would not make the household's connected story feel owned.
